draft.title: Aesthetic qualities and audience response
card: Aesthetic qualities are the beauty or power of a text's language, structure and images. They include sound, rhythm, striking pictures in words and the order in which a text is built.
These qualities shape how a reader or viewer feels. Short, sharp sentences can make a scene feel tense. Soft, flowing lines can make it feel calm.

Where and how a text is met also shapes the response. A poem read aloud in a hall can feel different from the same poem read silently alone. A film in a dark cinema can feel different from the same film on a phone.
To write about response, name the quality, give a short example from the text, then explain the effect on the audience.
draft.remember: Language, structure and images, and the setting where a text is met, all shape how an audience responds.

a.q: A story describes a storm in short, clipped sentences that build in pace. What is the likely effect on the reader?
opts: It creates tension and a feeling of urgency
It makes the scene feel slow and peaceful
It gives the reader a long, detailed history of storms
It makes the reader feel the storm is far away
a.why: Short, sharp sentences speed up the reading and can build tension. Slow and peaceful suits soft, flowing lines, which is the opposite of clipped sentences.
a.clue: Think about how quickly short sentences move.

b.q: Jess reads a quiet poem silently on her own at home. Her class later hears it read aloud at a school assembly. What best explains why her response may differ?
opts: The place and way it is met can change the response
The words of the poem change when it is read aloud
A poem can only have one effect on every audience
Reading aloud always makes a poem less powerful
b.why: The card says where and how a text is met can shape the response, such as silent reading compared with a hall. The words stay the same, so the wording is not the cause. The other options use absolutes the card does not support.
b.clue: The text stays the same, so look at what around it changes.

a.best: It creates tension and a feeling of urgency

b.best: The place and way it is met can change the response

problems.detail: The right option is the only one hedged with 'can', while two distractors use the absolutes 'only' and 'always'. A student could pick the answer by spotting the qualifier without knowing the idea.
The clue ('The text stays the same, so look at what around it changes') rules out the wording option and points straight to the setting option. It largely gives the answer away.

b.q: Jess reads a poem silently at home. Later she hears the exact same poem read aloud at assembly, and it moves her more. What best explains this?
opts: The setting and way she met the poem were different
The assembly reader changed some of the poem's words
Reading aloud takes away a poem's sound and rhythm
A poem's structure is rebuilt each time it is read
b.why: The poem's words stayed the same, so the change came from where and how Jess met it: silently alone, then aloud in a hall. Reading aloud does not take away sound and rhythm. Sound is one of the aesthetic qualities a listener hears.
b.clue: Compare the two times Jess met the poem.
